title: The Art of AI
answer: Ten creative disciplines and what artificial intelligence is doing inside each: how the work is made, what it runs on, who owns the result, and what is coming next.

children.name: Visual Arts and Generative Illustration
children.blurb: Prompt architecture, concept art, vector assets, inpainting and colour: the still image made with diffusion models.

children.name: Cinematography and Video Synthesis
children.blurb: Text to video, virtual lensing, digital doubles, storyboarding and frame interpolation.

children.name: Vocal Synthesis and Operatic Performance
children.blurb: Voice cloning, lip sync, emotional delivery, choral layering and live voice conversion.

children.name: Music Composition and Audio Engineering
children.blurb: Score generation, stem separation, drum programming, mixing and mastering, and generated foley.

children.name: Choreography and Motion Mapping
children.blurb: Kinematic generation, notation, motion capture retargeting, crowd simulation and biomechanics.

children.name: Literary Arts and Narrative Design
children.blurb: Agentic drafting, outlining, character dialogue, continuity tracking and developmental editing.

children.name: Theater and Virtual Set Design
children.blurb: Stage renderings, projection mapping, lighting plots, costume synthesis and acoustic modelling.

children.name: Photography and Hyper-Realism
children.blurb: Synthetic portraiture, lighting rigs, upscaling, product mockups and virtual location scouting.

children.name: Interactive and Experiential Art
children.blurb: Audience-reactive installations, generative AR and VR, dialogue engines, data sculptures and audio-visual systems.

children.name: Rights and Provenance in AI Art
children.blurb: Copyright and trademark, licensing, training data and opt-outs, studio security, and content credentials.

sections.body: This section is a field guide to ten creative disciplines where artificial intelligence is now part of the working process. It covers how the work is made, what hardware and software it runs on, who owns the result, and what is coming next. The pages move from still images and moving pictures to voice, music, dance, writing, theater, photography, interactive work, and the legal questions that follow all of them. The focus is on actual production, not theory: models that generate images, synthesize video, clone voices, compose audio, map motion, draft narrative, design sets, sharpen photographs, and respond to audiences. Each page describes the tools and workflows artists use today.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven and fast moving. Image and video generation are widely used, with this site tracking 1000 live image generation models and 1000 video models, but control, consistency, and factual accuracy remain hard problems. Audio is even more crowded, with 2000 audio models tracked, yet vocal synthesis and music composition still struggle with long form structure, emotional timing, and clean rights. The site also tracks 732 AI tools across these disciplines, which shows how much of the work is now tool driven rather than model driven. The honest limits are legal and technical: 92 active intellectual property lawsuits are tracked, 18 of them involving AI music services, and provenance, consent, and ownership are not settled. No page in this section claims the creative problem is solved.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The first two pages, Visual Arts and Generative Illustration and Cinematography and Video Synthesis, cover the most mature image and motion pipelines, from still frames to short films. Vocal Synthesis and Operatic Performance and Music Composition and Audio Engineering then move into sound, where the legal pressure is highest and the 18 AI music lawsuits are most relevant. Choreography and Motion Mapping and Theater and Virtual Set Design connect body movement and stage space to the same underlying pose and depth models. Literary Arts and Narrative Design and Photography and Hyper-Realism show two opposite pulls: language models that generate story and image models that erase the boundary between photograph and fiction. Interactive and Experiential Art describes live systems that respond to audiences, and Rights and Provenance in AI Art is the page to read last, because it explains who owns any of the work described in the other nine.
